Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Rohan is a 26-year-old South Asian man who works as an editor and is married. He has been experiencing significant distress following a traumatic event involving law enforcement. The incident occurred during one of his evening commutes when he witnessed a violent altercation between police officers and an individual in the street. Rohan had come to believe that the aggressive nature of the confrontation was unjustified, and this belief has continued to haunt him. Rohan vividly recalls the night of the incident—the cold winter air, the harsh glow of the streetlights, and the overwhelming grief he felt when he saw the victim on the ground. The smell of rain-soaked asphalt and gasoline still lingers in his memory whenever he thinks about that night. Since then, Rohan has been particularly sensitive to tactile sensations. A specific temperature on his skin can trigger a flood of memories, bringing him back to that cold evening. One day while working at his desk, Rohan felt the chill from an air conditioner and was suddenly transported back to that street corner. He began to feel detached, as though he were watching himself from afar. This dissociative feeling has become increasingly frequent, especially when he is alone with women, a trigger stemming from the presence of female officers during the incident. His ability to work effectively has been compromised by these intrusive memories and feelings. When Rohan tries to concentrate on his manuscripts, images of the event flash through his mind, and his body involuntarily reenacts the tension and fear he felt that night. He often finds himself tensing up or clenching his jaw, which distracts him from his tasks. Rohan has also started avoiding certain places and situations to minimize these triggers. He avoids going out on cold evenings and tries to work in a warmer environment to avoid the chill that brings back the memories. This avoidance has led to tension with his colleagues, as he often cancels last-minute meetings or refuses to go out for team lunches. The cumulative effect of these experiences is profound. Rohan had come to believe that his reactions since the event show that he is a lousy coper. He feels like he cannot handle simple tasks and has started questioning his role in life. The trauma has robbed him of any sense of meaning or purpose, leaving him feeling disconnected from both his work and his marriage. Rohan’s wife, Payal, notices that he is increasingly distant and preoccupied. She has tried to be supportive but often feels helpless when Rohan withdraws into himself. This emotional distance has created a rift in their relationship, leading them to have fewer meaningful conversations and shared moments. Despite these challenges, what frightens Rohan most is the belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore. He feels trapped by his thoughts and emotions, unable to envision a future where he might find joy or fulfillment again. It was the culmination of these distressing experiences that finally pushed Rohan to seek help. His wife suggested therapy after noticing how much his symptoms were affecting both their lives. In therapy, Rohan hopes to regain some sense of control over his life and work through the overwhelming grief and dissociation he feels when recalling the traumatic event. He is most hopeful for a future where he can find meaning again and reconnect with Payal on a deeper level.
